newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: IMF upbeat on global growth but wants more reform.
newsitem.headline: IMF upbeat on global growth but wants more reform.

text.p: International Monetary Fund Managing Director Michel Camdessus urged countries on Wednesday to do more on reform to keep up the momentum of favourable global economic growth.

Speaking at a meeting of the U.N. Economic and Social Council in Geneva, Camdessus said world economic growth would possibly pick up in 1997 over 1996 levels with even the poorest and least developed countries expected to do well.

Despite high unemployment in some European countries, he said prospects for growth were boosted by subdued global inflation, cuts in fiscal deficits, consistency in the exchange rates of major currencies and continuing structural reforms.
"Conditions are generally favourable for the expansion to continue at this pace, or a little faster in 1997 and over the medium-term," Camdessus said.

In 1996, Camdessus said Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew by an average 6.5 percent in real terms in the developing world -- the best performance in two decades -- and by 2.5 percent in the developed world. The global GDP growth rate was four percent.

Even the most under-developed nations improved their economic performance in 1996, with sub-Saharan Africa's GDP growing by 4.5 percent and heavily indebted poor countries and the least developed nations performing better still with average annual GDP growth rates of 5.5 percent, Camdessus said.
"(These are) levels they are expected to maintain over the medium term," he said.
But to sustain economic stabilisation, Camdessus said countries must do more on macro-economic stabilisation, trade liberalisation and privatisation.

"We have learnt that 'first generation' of reform is not, by itself, sufficient either to accelerate social progress or to allow countries to compete more successfully on global markets," Camdessus said.
He called for a "second generation of reforms" -- reforms with a human face to improve social policies, human resources, education and health systems and social safety nets.
Countries must be bolder in introducing structural reforms, Camdessus said.
Governments need to be more transparent and accountable to help boost private capital flows and domestic banking systems have to be strengthened, he added.
"The problem is that many of the obstacles to private sector initiative, job creation and foreign investment have been left in place. The solution is bolder, deeper reform," he said.

"Reforms of the second generation are absolutely indispensable if countries at all stages of development want to grasp the opportunities of globalisation and minimise risks and...accelerate the pace of human development."

Camdessus said the IMF was paying special attention to the soundness of banking systems and their potential risks to financial markets, to the quality of economic and financial data and to capital account liberalisation.
He gave no details on IMF's lending programmes.
